stimuli.title: The return of millets
stimuli.content:
Not long ago, millets such as ragi, jowar and bajra were dismissed in many Indian homes as 'poor man's food'. Rice and wheat, supported by assured government procurement and subsidised distribution, gradually took their place on the plate, and the area under millets shrank steadily over several decades. Today, however, these hardy grains are enjoying a revival, and the reasons are as much about health and climate as about taste.

Nutritionists point out that millets are rich in fibre, iron and calcium, and that they release sugar into the blood more slowly than polished rice. For a country with a rising number of people living with diabetes, this matters a great deal. Farmers, for their part, value millets because they grow on poor soils and need far less water than paddy. In regions where the monsoon is becoming less predictable, a crop that survives a dry spell can be the difference between a modest income and none at all.

The revival has not been easy, though. Millets are harder to process than rice or wheat; the small grains must be cleaned, de-husked and sometimes soaked before they can be cooked, and many villages lack the machines to do this. City consumers who are willing to pay more for millet biscuits and breakfast cereals often have little idea how to cook the grain itself. As a result, a large share of the price paid in a supermarket goes to processors and brands rather than to the farmer.

If the revival is to last, it will need more than enthusiasm. Small processing units close to the farms, fair procurement prices and recipes that suit modern kitchens could together turn a passing trend into a lasting change in what the country grows and eats. The humble millet, in short, deserves to be treated not as a fashion but as a foundation.

stimuli.title: The library that listened
stimuli.content:
For years, the district library in a small town in central India was a quiet, dusty building visited mainly by retired men reading the morning newspapers. Its shelves held old textbooks, its fans rarely worked, and its timings, ten in the morning to five in the evening, suited almost no one who had a job or attended college. Many residents assumed it would simply close one day without anyone noticing.

That changed when a new librarian decided to ask people what they actually wanted. The answers surprised her. Students preparing for competitive examinations wanted a quiet place to study and access to recent guidebooks they could not afford to buy. Young mothers wanted a corner where their children could read picture books. Daily-wage workers wanted help filling in online forms for government schemes. None of them had ever been asked before.

With a modest grant from the municipality and donations from local shops, the library extended its hours into the evening, set up a reading room for aspirants and installed four computers with an internet connection. Volunteers, many of them former students, offered to help visitors with forms and applications. Within two years, daily footfall rose from about thirty to more than four hundred, and a waiting list formed for seats in the reading room.

The story is not unique. Across the country, libraries that were once written off are finding new life by becoming community spaces rather than mere storehouses of books. Their success suggests a simple lesson that applies well beyond libraries: public institutions decline not only when they lack money but when they stop listening to the people they are meant to serve.

stimuli.title: Keeping it fresh
stimuli.content:
India is among the world's largest producers of fruits and vegetables, yet a significant share of what its farmers grow never reaches a consumer. Tomatoes split in the back of overloaded trucks, bananas ripen too early in hot warehouses, and leafy vegetables wilt while waiting for a buyer at a crowded market yard. Estimates of post-harvest loss vary, but even conservative figures suggest that the value lost every year is enormous.

The missing link is the cold chain: the unbroken sequence of pre-cooling, refrigerated storage and refrigerated transport that keeps perishable produce fresh from the farm gate to the retail shelf. A chain, as the name suggests, is only as useful as its weakest link. A cold store in a city is of little help if the produce has already spent eight hours in the sun on its way there. Much of the existing cold storage capacity, moreover, is concentrated in a few states and built for a single crop, the potato, which leaves growers of other perishables with few options.

Building more warehouses is therefore not the whole answer. What farmers need most is small pre-cooling and storage units close to where crops are harvested, along with refrigerated vehicles that can carry produce to distant markets. Such units are expensive to run on unreliable grid power, which is why solar-powered cold rooms that can be shared by a village have attracted attention. Farmer producer organisations, which pool the output of many small growers, are better placed than individual farmers to fill such facilities and to bargain with buyers.

Storage alone, however, does not guarantee a better price. A farmer who can hold back his tomatoes for two weeks gains only if he knows where and when prices will rise, and has the means to reach that market. Information, finance and logistics must therefore advance together. When they do, a cold chain does more than prevent waste: it gives the grower the one thing he has rarely had, the freedom to choose when to sell.

stimuli.title: The missing middle
stimuli.content:
India's health financing has long had an odd shape. The poorest households are covered, at least on paper, by government-funded insurance schemes, while salaried employees in the formal sector usually receive a policy from their employer. Between these two groups lies a large population of shopkeepers, small traders, self-employed professionals and informal workers who are too well-off to qualify for free schemes but not well-off enough to feel that they can afford private cover. Policy researchers call them the 'missing middle'.

For these households, a single hospital admission can wipe out years of savings. Yet many of them do not buy insurance even when a suitable policy is available at a modest premium. The reasons are partly financial and partly psychological. A premium is a certain cost paid today, while an illness is an uncertain event that may never happen, and people tend to give more weight to the first than to the second. Some also see an unused policy as money wasted, much as one might regret buying an umbrella in a year without rain. Others simply distrust insurers, having heard stories of claims rejected on technical grounds.

Insurers have responded with cheaper products, shorter forms and cashless treatment at network hospitals, but take-up has risen only slowly. Experience from other countries suggests that what works best is a combination of measures: making enrolment simple, perhaps through a bank account or a mobile app; pooling small buyers into groups so that premiums fall; and settling claims quickly and transparently so that trust can be built over time.

None of these steps is dramatic. Together, however, they address the real obstacle, which is less the price of a policy than the belief that it will be there when needed. A household that has seen a neighbour's claim paid without fuss is far more likely to buy a policy than one that has only seen an advertisement.

stimuli.title: The power of the default
stimuli.content:
Economics textbooks once assumed that people, given the right information, would make the choices that best served their long-term interests. If saving for retirement was sensible, rational workers would save. Decades of evidence have complicated that picture. People procrastinate, are swayed by how options are presented and, above all, tend to stick with whatever happens if they do nothing. This last tendency, the power of the default, has become one of the most studied ideas in public policy.

Consider a pension scheme in which employees must fill in a form to join. Many who intend to enrol never get round to it, not because they have weighed the scheme and rejected it but because the form sits on a desk for months. Reverse the arrangement, so that employees are enrolled automatically unless they choose to opt out, and participation typically rises sharply, even though the scheme itself has not changed in the slightest. Nobody is forced to save; the path of least resistance has merely been redrawn.

Supporters of such 'nudges' argue that they preserve freedom while correcting predictable lapses. Critics are less comfortable. A default, they point out, is never neutral: someone must choose it, and that someone may have interests of their own. A default contribution rate set too low may leave workers falsely reassured that they are saving enough; a default investment fund chosen for the provider's convenience may serve the provider better than the saver. There is also the question of consent. A choice that people make only because they did not notice they were making it is a curious kind of choice.

The sensible conclusion is not to abandon defaults, which are unavoidable in any case, since every form must begin somewhere, but to design them with care and disclose them openly. If inertia is going to decide outcomes for millions of people, those who set the starting point bear a responsibility that is easy to underestimate precisely because it is so quiet.

stimuli.title: A net or a hammock
stimuli.content:
Deposit insurance is one of the quiet foundations of modern banking. By promising that ordinary depositors will get their money back, up to a fixed limit, even if their bank fails, it removes the main reason for a bank run: the fear that those who wait in the queue will be left with nothing. A rumour that might once have emptied a sound bank in an afternoon now does far less damage, because small savers know their deposits are safe.

Yet the same protection creates a subtler problem, which economists call moral hazard. When people are shielded from the consequences of a risk, they tend to take less care to avoid it. An insured depositor has little reason to ask whether her bank lends prudently, and a bank that knows its depositors will not desert it may be tempted to chase high returns through risky loans. The guarantee that prevents panic can thus weaken the discipline that would otherwise keep banks careful.

Policymakers have tried to strike a balance. Coverage is usually capped, so that large depositors, who are better able to monitor a bank, still bear some risk. Banks pay premiums for the insurance, and some systems charge higher premiums to riskier banks, much as a careless driver pays more for motor insurance. Above all, deposit insurance is paired with regulation and supervision: if depositors no longer watch the banks closely, someone else must.

The arrangement is therefore less a single safety net than a bargain. Society agrees to protect small savers from the failure of institutions they cannot be expected to understand; in return, banks accept rules on capital, liquidity and lending that limit their freedom to gamble with insured money. When either side of that bargain weakens, when coverage expands without matching supervision or when supervisors grow complacent, the safety net can quietly turn into a hammock.

stimuli.title: The bicycle comes back
stimuli.content:
In many Indian cities, the bicycle was once the most common way to get to work. Mill workers, clerks and students rode to their (1) ______ every morning, and a bicycle was a prized possession that was passed down from parent to child. As incomes rose, however, the scooter and the car gradually (2) ______ it, and the cycle came to be seen as a sign of poverty rather than of good sense.

Today, as traffic jams grow longer and the air in many cities becomes harder to breathe, planners are taking a fresh look at this simple machine. A bicycle produces no fumes, takes up little road space and costs almost nothing to run. Regular cycling also keeps the rider fit, which is a real (3) ______ at a time when lifestyle diseases are rising.

The main obstacle is safety. Few people are willing to ride alongside speeding buses and trucks, and most roads offer no separate space for cyclists. Where cities have built protected cycle lanes and secure parking, the number of riders has (4) ______ quickly. Some cities have also introduced public bicycle-sharing schemes, under which a cycle can be hired at one station and returned at another for a small fee.

Such schemes work best when they are (5) ______ to bus and metro stations, so that a commuter can ride the first and last kilometre of the journey. The bicycle will not replace the bus or the train, but it can make them far more useful. A city that makes room for cyclists, in short, makes room for everyone.

stimuli.title: Weavers on the web
stimuli.content:
For generations, handloom weavers in India sold their saris and fabrics through middlemen who bought cheaply in the village and sold at a large profit in the city. The weaver, who might spend weeks on a single piece, rarely knew what the final buyer paid for it. Online marketplaces and social media have begun to (1) ______ this pattern. A weaver with a smartphone can now photograph her work, describe how it was made and sell it directly to a customer hundreds of kilometres away.

The benefits can be (2) ______. Weavers who sell directly report earning noticeably more per piece, and some have built a loyal following among buyers who value the story behind each product. Customers, for their part, gain access to genuine handwoven goods instead of cheaper machine-made (3) ______ that are often passed off as handloom.

Selling online, however, brings new demands. Photographs must be clear, descriptions accurate and parcels packed so that delicate fabric is not damaged. Payments, returns and customer queries must be handled promptly, and a single bad review can (4) ______ sales for weeks. Many weavers, especially older ones, find these tasks daunting and continue to depend on intermediaries.

Weavers' cooperatives and a few non-profit groups are trying to meet this need by offering training in photography, digital payments and basic bookkeeping, and by handling packing and dispatch collectively. Their experience suggests that technology works best when it is (5) ______ by support on the ground. A website can open a door, but someone still has to help the weaver walk through it.

stimuli.title: Learning by doing
stimuli.content:
Every year, millions of young Indians finish school or college with a certificate but little idea of how a workplace actually functions. Employers, in turn, complain that graduates lack practical skills and must be trained almost from scratch. Apprenticeships, in which a young person learns a trade by working under experienced staff while earning a stipend, offer a way to (1) ______ young people with real experience before they enter the job market.

The idea is old. Carpenters, goldsmiths and tailors have always learned by watching and assisting a master. What is new is the attempt to make apprenticeships a formal (2) ______ to employment across industries, from retail and hospitality to banking and manufacturing. For the apprentice, the arrangement offers income, experience and a credential that employers recognise. For the firm, it offers a chance to train future staff in its own methods and to judge their ability before making a permanent offer.

Yet the numbers remain modest compared with the size of the workforce. Small firms, which employ most workers, often find the paperwork (3) ______ and fear that an apprentice will leave as soon as the training is complete. Some larger firms, meanwhile, have been accused of using apprentices as cheap labour, assigning them routine tasks that teach them little.

Making the system work will require simpler rules, so that a small workshop can take on an apprentice without hiring a consultant, and closer (4) ______ of what apprentices actually learn. Industry bodies can help by designing short, practical courses and by certifying skills in a way that is recognised across firms. An apprenticeship that ends with a certificate no one trusts is little better than a degree no one values. If these conditions are met, apprenticeships could become one of the most (5) ______ routes into work for young people who want to learn by doing.

stimuli.title: Too many visitors
stimuli.content:
Every summer, the roads leading to popular hill towns fill with cars, and towns built for a few thousand residents find themselves hosting many times that number of visitors. Hotels are booked out, water tankers run day and night, and garbage piles up faster than the local body can (1) ______ it. What was once a quiet retreat begins to resemble the crowded city the tourists came to escape.

Tourism is, of course, a vital source of income for these regions, where farming is difficult and industry scarce. The problem is not tourism itself but its (2) ______: too many visitors arriving in the same few weeks, staying in the same few places and making demands that fragile mountain slopes cannot bear. Unplanned construction of hotels on steep slopes has made some towns more (3) ______ to landslides, and the loss of forest cover has worsened the damage caused by heavy rain.

Some local governments have begun to experiment with limits. A few have introduced permits for vehicles entering ecologically sensitive areas, while others charge a small green fee whose proceeds are spent on waste management. Promoting lesser-known destinations and off-season travel can also spread visitors more evenly through the year.

Such measures are rarely popular at first. Hotel owners worry about losing business, and visitors resent paying for what was once free. But the alternative is a slow decline in which the very beauty that draws tourists is (4) ______ by their numbers. A hill town that protects its forests, water and slopes is not turning tourists away; it is making sure there will still be something worth visiting in twenty years.

stimuli.title: What your deposit really earns
stimuli.content:
For millions of households, a fixed deposit is the simplest way to save. The interest rate printed on the deposit receipt, however, can be **(1) misleading**. What matters to a saver is not the nominal rate but the real rate: the return left after inflation has been taken into account. If a deposit earns seven per cent a year while prices rise by six per cent, the saver's purchasing power grows by only about one per cent, and if inflation **(2) falls** above the deposit rate, the saver is in effect becoming poorer every year even as the balance on paper keeps rising.

This distinction matters most for those who depend on interest income, such as retired people. When inflation is high and deposit rates lag behind, they face an uncomfortable choice: accept a **(3) gain** in their real income or move their savings into riskier assets in search of higher returns. Many choose the second path without fully understanding the risks, which is one reason why the mis-selling of complex products tends to rise when real rates are **(4) generous**.

Tax adds another layer. Interest on deposits is generally taxed as income, so the post-tax real return can be lower still, or even negative for savers in higher tax brackets. A saver who looks only at the headline rate may therefore greatly overestimate how much her money is really earning.

None of this means that deposits are a poor choice; they remain safe, liquid and easy to understand. It does mean that savers should judge them by the right yardstick. The question to ask is not 'How much interest will I get?' but 'How much more will my money be able to buy at the end of the year?'

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, why did rice and wheat gradually replace millets on Indian plates?

options.text: Millets were banned from village markets.
Rice and wheat were backed by assured procurement and subsidised distribution.
Farmers found that millets needed too much water.
Millets could not be grown on poor soils.

solution.concept: Locating a stated reason
solution.explanation: The first paragraph says rice and wheat, 'supported by assured government procurement and subsidised distribution', gradually took the place of millets.
steps: Find the sentence about rice and wheat in paragraph 1
The reason given is government support: procurement and subsidised distribution
solution.why_others_wrong: A: no ban is mentioned. C and D reverse the passage, which says millets need far less water than paddy and grow on poor soils.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Rice and wheat were backed by assured procurement and subsidised distribution.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as an advantage of millets?

options.text: They are rich in fibre, iron and calcium.
They release sugar into the blood more slowly than polished rice.
They grow on poor soils and need far less water than paddy.
They fetch farmers a higher share of the supermarket price than rice does.

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question: eliminate every option the passage states
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists the nutritional and farming advantages in A, B and C. Paragraph 3 says the opposite of D: a large share of the supermarket price goes to processors and brands rather than to the farmer.
steps: Paragraph 2: fibre, iron, calcium (A); slow sugar release (B); poor soils, less water (C)
Paragraph 3: most of the retail price does not reach the farmer
So D is not an advantage stated: answer D
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are all stated as advantages in paragraph 2, so none of them can be the 'NOT mentioned' answer.
solution.final_answer: Option D: They fetch farmers a higher share of the supermarket price than rice does.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, does a large share of the price paid for millet products not reach the farmer?

options.text: Farmers sell their grain directly to city consumers.
The government fixes a very low retail price for millet products.
Processing is difficult, and much of the value is captured by processors and brands.
Millets spoil quickly and must be sold cheaply.

solution.concept: Linking a result ('As a result') to the reasons before it
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 explains that millets are hard to process, villages lack machines and city buyers purchase processed goods such as biscuits. 'As a result', the money goes to processors and brands. Option C joins these points.
steps: Find 'As a result' in paragraph 3 and read the sentences before it
Causes: hard processing, no village machines, buyers want processed products
Effect: value goes to processors and brands: option C
solution.why_others_wrong: A contradicts the passage: the sale is through supermarkets and brands, not direct. B (government retail price) and D (quick spoilage) are never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Processing is difficult, and much of the value is captured by processors and brands.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is most similar in meaning to the word 'hardy' as used in the passage ('these hardy grains')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: hardy = able to survive difficult conditions
solution.explanation: The passage says millets grow on poor soils, need little water and survive dry spells. A 'hardy' crop is tough and able to withstand hard conditions, so 'robust' is closest.
steps: Look for clues: poor soils, little water, survives a dry spell
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Fragile' is the opposite. 'Expensive' and 'tasty' are not suggested by the passage's description of how millets grow.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, why did the library's old timings suit almost no one?

options.text: They clashed with the hours of people who had jobs or attended college.
The library opened only on weekends.
The building had no electricity in the evening.

solution.concept: Locating a stated fact
solution.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the timings, ten to five, 'suited almost no one who had a job or attended college': these people were busy during exactly those hours.
steps: Ten to five overlaps with working and college hours
solution.why_others_wrong: B, C and D are never mentioned. The passage mentions fans that rarely worked, not a lack of electricity, and says nothing about the old librarian's attendance.
solution.final_answer: Option A: They clashed with the hours of people who had jobs or attended college.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following was NOT one of the changes made by the library?

options.text: Extending its hours into the evening
Setting up a reading room for aspirants
Installing computers with an internet connection
Charging a membership fee to cover its costs

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists the changes: longer hours, a reading room and four computers with internet. The money came from a municipal grant and shop donations; no membership fee is mentioned.
steps: List the changes in paragraph 3: hours, reading room, computers
A membership fee is not mentioned: D
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are all named in paragraph 3 as changes the library made.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Charging a membership fee to cover its costs

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What did the daily-wage workers want from the library?

options.text: Help filling in online forms for government schemes

solution.concept: Matching each group to its stated need
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 says daily-wage workers 'wanted help filling in online forms for government schemes'.
steps: Paragraph 2 lists three groups and their needs
Daily-wage workers → help with online forms
solution.why_others_wrong: A is what young mothers wanted. C and D are what students preparing for examinations wanted.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Help filling in online forms for government schemes

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following does the passage suggest was the main reason for the library's revival?

options.text: A large grant from the state government
The supply of free newspapers to all visitors
The librarian asked people what they needed and the library responded to those needs
The closure of other libraries in the district

solution.concept: Inference: identify the turning point and the author's own conclusion
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 says things 'changed when a new librarian decided to ask people what they actually wanted', and every change in paragraph 3 answers one of those wants. The final sentence makes listening the key lesson.
steps: Turning point: the librarian asks people what they want
Changes made match the needs people expressed
Conclusion: institutions decline when they stop listening
So listening and responding drove the revival: C
solution.why_others_wrong: A: the grant was 'modest' and came from the municipality, not the state. B: newspapers belong to the old, declining library. D: no other library closure is mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The librarian asked people what they needed and the library responded to those needs

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best expresses the central lesson the author draws from the story?

options.text: Libraries should replace books with computers.
Small towns no longer need public libraries.
Volunteers can run public institutions without any funding.
Public institutions thrive when they listen and respond to the people they serve.

solution.concept: Main idea: the lesson is stated in the concluding sentence
solution.explanation: The last sentence says public institutions decline 'when they stop listening to the people they are meant to serve'. The positive form of this lesson is option D.
steps: Read the final paragraph: 'a simple lesson that applies well beyond libraries'
Lesson: institutions decline when they stop listening
solution.why_others_wrong: A: computers were only one change; books remained. B is contradicted by the rise in footfall. C ignores the municipal grant and shop donations.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Public institutions thrive when they listen and respond to the people they serve.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, why is much of the existing cold storage of limited use to many growers?

options.text: It is located only near ports.
It is concentrated in a few states and built mainly for potatoes.
It is too cheap to be maintained properly.
It is reserved for produce meant for export.

solution.concept: Locating a stated fact
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 says existing capacity 'is concentrated in a few states and built for a single crop, the potato, which leaves growers of other perishables with few options'.
steps: Find 'existing cold storage capacity' in paragraph 2
Two limits: few states, one crop (potato)
solution.why_others_wrong: Ports (A), low cost (C) and export (D) are not mentioned anywhere in the passage.
solution.final_answer: Option B: It is concentrated in a few states and built mainly for potatoes.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: The statement 'A chain ... is only as useful as its weakest link' is used in the passage to suggest that

options.text: a single gap in the sequence can undo the benefit of all the other links
cold stores in cities are unnecessary
refrigerated trucks are the most important part of the chain
farmers should avoid selling in distant markets

solution.concept: Inference: understand the purpose of an image by reading the example that follows it
solution.explanation: The very next sentence gives the example: a city cold store is of little help if the produce has already spent eight hours in the sun. One broken link (no pre-cooling or cool transport) wastes the rest.
steps: Read the example after the image
Good storage at the end cannot save produce damaged earlier
So one weak link spoils the whole chain: A
solution.why_others_wrong: B overstates: the passage says a city store is of little help only when earlier links fail. C picks one link as most important, which the image denies. D contradicts the passage, which wants produce carried to distant markets.
solution.final_answer: Option A: a single gap in the sequence can undo the benefit of all the other links

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, are farmer producer organisations well placed to use cold-chain facilities?

options.text: They receive free electricity from the grid.
They own most of the cold stores in cities.
They are allowed to fix retail prices.
They pool the output of many growers, so they can fill facilities and bargain with buyers.

solution.concept: Locating a stated reason
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 says these organisations 'pool the output of many small growers' and are therefore 'better placed than individual farmers to fill such facilities and to bargain with buyers'.
solution.why_others_wrong: A contradicts the passage, which calls grid power unreliable and costly. B and C are never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option D: They pool the output of many growers, so they can fill facilities and bargain with buyers.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following can be inferred about a farmer who has access to storage but no information about markets?

options.text: He can safely ignore price movements.
He will always earn more than a farmer without storage.
He may gain little from storage, since he cannot tell when or where to sell profitably.
He will no longer need any finance.

solution.concept: Inference from a conditional statement ('gains only if ...')
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 says a farmer who holds back his produce 'gains only if he knows where and when prices will rise'. Without that knowledge, storage by itself may bring little benefit.
steps: Key sentence: 'Storage alone ... does not guarantee a better price'
Condition for gain: knowing where and when prices rise
No information → the condition fails → little gain: C
solution.why_others_wrong: A and B contradict 'gains only if he knows'. D contradicts the passage, which says information, finance and logistics must advance together.
solution.final_answer: Option C: He may gain little from storage, since he cannot tell when or where to sell profitably.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'conservative' as used in the passage ('even conservative figures suggest')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: a word with several meanings
solution.explanation: 'Conservative figures' are deliberately low, cautious estimates. 'Even' cautious figures show a large loss, so the true loss may be larger still. 'Cautious' fits.
steps: 'even conservative figures' = even the lowest, most careful estimates
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Traditional' and 'political' are other senses of 'conservative' that do not fit figures. 'Exaggerated' is the opposite of the meaning here.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?

options.text: Potatoes and the Politics of Storage
Keeping It Fresh: Why the Cold Chain Needs More Than Cold Stores

solution.concept: A title must cover the whole passage
solution.explanation: The passage describes post-harvest loss, explains the cold chain, argues that small local units matter more than big warehouses and adds that information and finance are also needed. Option D captures the topic and the argument.
steps: Para 1: losses; para 2: the cold chain and its gaps
Para 3: more warehouses are not enough; para 4: information and finance too
solution.why_others_wrong: A and C each pick up a single detail. B contradicts the conclusion, which values the freedom to choose when to sell.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Keeping It Fresh: Why the Cold Chain Needs More Than Cold Stores

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Who, according to the passage, make up the 'missing middle'?

options.text: Households too well-off for free schemes but not confident that they can afford private cover
Salaried employees of large firms in the formal sector
Households covered by both government and employer insurance

solution.concept: Locating a definition
solution.explanation: Paragraph 1 defines the group as those 'too well-off to qualify for free schemes but not well-off enough to feel that they can afford private cover'.
steps: Find the term 'missing middle' at the end of paragraph 1
Read the sentence before it: the definition
solution.why_others_wrong: B and C are the two groups on either side of the missing middle, both of which have some cover. D describes no group in the passage.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Households too well-off for free schemes but not confident that they can afford private cover

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: The comparison with 'buying an umbrella in a year without rain' is meant to illustrate

options.text: that insurance premiums rise in bad years
the feeling that a policy which is never claimed has been a waste of money
that insurers reject claims on technical grounds
that households should save instead of buying insurance

solution.concept: Inference: the purpose of an analogy
solution.explanation: The sentence says some people 'see an unused policy as money wasted, much as one might regret buying an umbrella in a year without rain'. An unused umbrella, like an unclaimed policy, feels wasted, even though it was sensible protection.
steps: Read the full sentence containing the analogy
Shared feeling: regret over money 'wasted': B
solution.why_others_wrong: A: premiums are not discussed. C is a separate reason given in the next sentence. D is not the author's advice; the passage argues for more insurance.
solution.final_answer: Option B: the feeling that a policy which is never claimed has been a waste of money

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT among the measures that, according to the passage, have worked best in other countries?

options.text: Making enrolment simple through a bank account or a mobile app
Pooling small buyers into groups so that premiums fall
Making insurance compulsory for all self-employed people

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists three measures: simple enrolment, pooling buyers into groups and quick, transparent claim settlement. Compulsion is never mentioned.
steps: Find 'Experience from other countries' in paragraph 3
Compulsory insurance is not among them: C
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and D are the three measures listed in paragraph 3.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Making insurance compulsory for all self-employed people

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the author, the main obstacle to insurance take-up among these households is

options.text: doubt that the policy will actually pay out when it is needed

solution.concept: Identifying the author's main claim ('the real obstacle')
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the real obstacle 'is less the price of a policy than the belief that it will be there when needed'. The example of a neighbour's claim being paid shows that trust is what matters.
steps: 'less the price ... than the belief that it will be there when needed'
So the obstacle is doubt about payment: D
solution.why_others_wrong: A is explicitly ranked below trust ('less the price'). B and C are mentioned only as problems insurers have already addressed, without much effect.
solution.final_answer: Option D: doubt that the policy will actually pay out when it is needed

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, does automatic enrolment raise participation even though the scheme is unchanged?

options.text: Workers are legally barred from leaving the scheme.
Automatic enrolment comes with a higher rate of return.
Many people who intend to join never act, and automatic enrolment turns their inaction into saving.
Most non-participants had rejected the scheme after careful thought.

solution.concept: Inference: connect the example to the general tendency (inertia)
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 says many who intend to enrol never do so because the form sits on a desk, not because they reject the scheme. When enrolment is automatic, the same inaction keeps them in. People 'stick with whatever happens if they do nothing'.
steps: Paragraph 1: people stick with the default
Paragraph 2: non-joiners are procrastinators, not rejecters
Automatic enrolment makes doing nothing = saving: C
solution.why_others_wrong: A contradicts 'unless they choose to opt out' and 'Nobody is forced to save'. B contradicts 'the scheme itself has not changed'. D is the opposite of what the passage says ('not because they have weighed the scheme and rejected it').
solution.final_answer: Option C: Many people who intend to join never act, and automatic enrolment turns their inaction into saving.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following statements would the critics mentioned in the passage most likely agree with?

options.text: Defaults should be banned from all public schemes.
Whoever sets a default can shape outcomes in ways that may not serve the saver.
Nudges take away workers' freedom to leave a scheme.
People always make rational choices when they are given enough information.

solution.concept: Inference: extend a viewpoint without overstating it
solution.explanation: The critics say a default 'is never neutral: someone must choose it, and that someone may have interests of their own', and give examples of low contribution rates and provider-friendly funds. Option B summarises this concern.
steps: Locate the critics' view in paragraph 3
Core concern: the person who sets the default may not act for the saver
solution.why_others_wrong: A is too extreme; the critics question defaults but never call for a ban, and the author notes defaults are unavoidable. C misstates the scheme: workers can opt out. D is the old textbook assumption that the passage says has been 'complicated'.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Whoever sets a default can shape outcomes in ways that may not serve the saver.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: The author's attitude towards defaults is best described as

options.text: cautiously accepting: defaults are unavoidable, but they must be designed carefully and disclosed

solution.concept: Author's attitude: read the concluding paragraph
solution.explanation: The author rejects abandoning defaults ('unavoidable in any case') but insists they be designed 'with care' and disclosed 'openly', stressing the responsibility of those who set them. That is cautious acceptance.
steps: Para 2 presents the benefit of defaults; para 3 presents the critics' concerns
Para 4: keep defaults but design and disclose them carefully
solution.why_others_wrong: B ignores the author's warnings about responsibility. C ignores the author's view that defaults are unavoidable and useful. D does not fit an author who draws a firm conclusion and speaks of responsibility.
solution.final_answer: Option A: cautiously accepting: defaults are unavoidable, but they must be designed carefully and disclosed

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the author mean by saying that the responsibility of those who set defaults is 'easy to underestimate precisely because it is so quiet'?

options.text: The officials who set defaults rarely speak in public.
Defaults affect only a small number of people.
Pension providers deliberately hide their fees from savers.
Defaults work unnoticed, so their large influence on outcomes is seldom recognised.

solution.concept: Inference: interpret figurative language in context
solution.explanation: A default decides outcomes for millions of people who simply do nothing; no one notices a decision being made. Because its influence is silent, people underestimate how much power the person who sets it holds.
steps: Preceding clause: inertia decides outcomes 'for millions of people'
Large influence + no notice = easily underestimated: D
solution.why_others_wrong: A takes 'quiet' literally. B contradicts 'millions of people'. C introduces fees, which the passage never mentions.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Defaults work unnoticed, so their large influence on outcomes is seldom recognised.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, how does deposit insurance prevent bank runs?

options.text: It reassures small savers that their deposits are safe even if the bank fails, so they have no reason to rush to withdraw.
It forbids depositors to withdraw money during a crisis.
It guarantees depositors a higher rate of interest.
It makes large depositors bear the entire risk of failure.

solution.concept: Locating a stated mechanism
solution.explanation: Paragraph 1 says insurance removes 'the main reason for a bank run: the fear that those who wait in the queue will be left with nothing', because small savers know their deposits are safe.
steps: Cause of a run: fear that latecomers lose everything
So savers do not rush: A
solution.why_others_wrong: B and C are never mentioned. D distorts paragraph 3: large depositors bear 'some' risk because coverage is capped, not the entire risk.
solution.final_answer: Option A: It reassures small savers that their deposits are safe even if the bank fails, so they have no reason to rush to withdraw.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of moral hazard as the passage describes it?

options.text: A false rumour makes depositors queue outside a sound bank.
A large depositor moves money out of a bank whose lending looks risky.
A bank expands risky, high-return lending because it knows its insured depositors will not withdraw.
A regulator raises the capital that banks must hold.

solution.concept: Applying a defined concept to a new case
solution.explanation: Moral hazard is taking less care because one is shielded from the consequences. Paragraph 2 says a bank that knows its depositors will not desert it 'may be tempted to chase high returns through risky loans'. Option C is that behaviour.
steps: Definition: protection from a risk → less care to avoid it
Who is protected? Depositors (insured) and so, indirectly, the bank's funding
Option C shows the bank taking more risk because of that protection
solution.why_others_wrong: A describes the panic that insurance prevents, not moral hazard. B shows market discipline, the opposite of moral hazard. D is a regulatory response to moral hazard.
solution.final_answer: Option C: A bank expands risky, high-return lending because it knows its insured depositors will not withdraw.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, why is deposit insurance coverage usually capped?

options.text: To make sure the insurer never runs out of funds
So that large depositors, who can monitor banks better, still bear some risk
To discourage wealthy people from saving in banks
Because small savers do not need protection

solution.concept: Answer from the passage's stated reason, not from outside knowledge
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 gives the reason directly: coverage is capped 'so that large depositors, who are better able to monitor a bank, still bear some risk'. Their exposure keeps some market discipline alive.
steps: Find 'Coverage is usually capped' in paragraph 3
Read the 'so that' clause: the stated purpose
solution.why_others_wrong: A may be true in the real world but is not the reason the passage gives. C misreads the purpose. D contradicts the passage, whose whole point is protecting small savers.
solution.final_answer: Option B: So that large depositors, who can monitor banks better, still bear some risk

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the author suggest by saying that the safety net can 'quietly turn into a hammock'?

options.text: Deposit insurance will eventually be withdrawn.
Banks will become too small to fail.
Depositors will stop earning interest on their savings.
A protection meant to catch failures can instead encourage complacency and comfortable risk-taking.

solution.concept: Interpreting a concluding metaphor
solution.explanation: A safety net catches someone who falls; a hammock is something one lies back in comfortably. If supervision weakens, insurance stops being an emergency protection and becomes a comfort that lets banks and supervisors relax and take risks: the moral hazard of paragraph 2.
steps: Net = catches failures; hammock = encourages relaxing
The sentence names the conditions: coverage without supervision, complacent supervisors
So protection turns into complacency: D
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C read meanings into the metaphor that the passage never discusses (withdrawal of insurance, bank size, interest).
solution.final_answer: Option D: A protection meant to catch failures can instead encourage complacency and comfortable risk-taking.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: what one rides 'to'
solution.explanation: Workers and students rode their bicycles to the places they had to reach every morning: their destinations (factories, offices, colleges).
solution.why_others_wrong: One does not ride 'to' one's vehicles, journeys or accidents; none of these is a place reached every morning.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the contrast set up by 'however'
solution.explanation: The bicycle was once the most common vehicle; 'however', as incomes rose, scooters and cars took its place and it came to be seen as a sign of poverty. 'Replaced' expresses this.
steps: 'However' signals a change from the bicycle's earlier popularity
Scooters and cars took its place
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Rescued' and 'repaired' would be positive actions on the bicycle, which do not explain its fall in status. 'Rented' makes no sense with scooters and cars as the subject.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: tone of the paragraph (benefits of cycling)
solution.explanation: The paragraph lists the bicycle's benefits: no fumes, little road space, low cost. Keeping riders fit when lifestyle diseases are rising is another benefit, so 'advantage' fits.
steps: Fitness during a rise in lifestyle diseases is a positive
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Burden', 'expense' and 'risk' are negatives and contradict the list of benefits.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: cause and effect
solution.explanation: Safety is the main obstacle. Where cities removed it with protected lanes and parking, more people started cycling: the number of riders 'has risen quickly'.
steps: Protected lanes and parking remove the obstacle
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Fallen' reverses the effect of safer roads. 'Stopped' and 'frozen' do not go with 'quickly' and make no sense as a result of better facilities.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'so that' gives the purpose
solution.explanation: Sharing schemes help a commuter ride 'the first and last kilometre' to and from a bus or metro station. That works only if the cycle stations are linked to bus and metro stations.
steps: Purpose clause: 'so that a commuter can ride the first and last kilometre'
The cycle must connect with the bus or metro
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Opposed to', 'unknown to' and 'closed to' would all prevent commuters from using the bicycles with buses and trains, defeating the purpose stated after 'so that'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the new development contrasts with the old pattern
solution.explanation: The old pattern was selling through middlemen. Online selling lets weavers sell directly, so it has begun to change that pattern.
steps: Old pattern: middlemen take the profit
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Repeat' and 'protect' would keep the middleman system, which the next sentence shows is being bypassed. 'Admire' makes no sense with 'this pattern' here.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the sentences that follow decide the word
solution.explanation: The next sentences describe clear gains: noticeably higher earnings, loyal buyers and genuine goods for customers. So the benefits are 'substantial'.
steps: Read ahead: 'earning noticeably more per piece', 'a loyal following'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Negligible' and 'imaginary' deny the gains that follow. 'Harmful' contradicts the word 'benefits'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: contrast between genuine and fake goods
solution.explanation: Customers get 'genuine handwoven goods instead of cheaper machine-made imitations that are often passed off as handloom'. Something 'passed off' as handloom is an imitation.
steps: 'passed off as handloom' = pretending to be handloom
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Machines' are not sold as fabric. 'Originals' contradicts 'passed off as'. 'Weavers' are people, not goods.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the paragraph lists difficulties
solution.explanation: The paragraph describes the demands and risks of selling online. A single bad review is one such risk: it can hurt sales for weeks.
steps: A bad review has a negative effect
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Boost' and 'double' are positive effects, which a bad review does not cause. 'Fix sales for weeks' is meaningless here.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the closing image explains the blank
solution.explanation: Cooperatives give training and handle packing alongside online selling. The lesson is that technology works best when it is backed (supported) by help on the ground, which the final sentence repeats: a website opens a door, but someone must help the weaver through it.
steps: Cooperatives add human support to the technology
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Replaced by support' would remove the technology, but the final sentence keeps the website. 'Opposed' and 'delayed' contradict the cooperatives' helpful role.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: verb pattern 'provide someone with something'
solution.explanation: Apprenticeships give young people practical experience, which they otherwise lack. 'Provide young people with real experience' fits both the meaning and the preposition 'with'.
steps: Problem in the paragraph: graduates lack practical skills
Apprenticeships solve it by giving experience
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Deprive' means the opposite and takes 'of'. 'Threaten young people with experience' and 'charge young people with experience' are illogical here.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: noun + 'to employment'
solution.explanation: The paragraph presents apprenticeships as a route into jobs: income, a recognised credential and a chance of a permanent offer. 'A formal pathway to employment' fits.
steps: The noun must mean a route
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Barrier' and 'obstacle' would mean apprenticeships block jobs, which contradicts the paragraph. 'Substitute' takes 'for' and would mean apprenticeships replace employment.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: a reason for low uptake by small firms
solution.explanation: The paragraph explains why numbers stay modest. Small firms find the paperwork burdensome; the last paragraph confirms this by calling for simpler rules so a workshop need not hire a consultant.
steps: Paragraph topic: why few firms take apprentices
Confirmed later: 'simpler rules ... without hiring a consultant': 'burdensome'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Rewarding' and 'simple' would encourage firms, not deter them. 'Optional' paperwork would not be a problem either.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: a remedy for the problem described earlier
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 says some firms use apprentices as cheap labour on tasks that teach little. The remedy is closer monitoring of what apprentices actually learn.
steps: Problem: apprentices learn little in some firms
'closer monitoring of what apprentices actually learn'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Closer neglect' is self-contradictory and would worsen the problem. 'Imitation' and 'celebration' of what apprentices learn do not address it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'If these conditions are met' signals a positive outcome
solution.explanation: The sentence describes what happens once the problems are fixed, so the outcome must be positive: apprenticeships could become one of the most promising routes into work.
steps: Condition: the fixes in this paragraph are made
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Neglected', 'costly' and 'uncertain' are negative outcomes, which do not follow from meeting the conditions.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the job a local body does with garbage
solution.explanation: Garbage 'piles up faster than the local body can clear it': the municipality removes garbage, and crowds create it faster than it can be removed.
steps: The local body's role: removing it
solution.why_others_wrong: A local body does not 'produce' or 'admire' garbage. 'Count it' does not explain why garbage piles up.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the explanation after the colon defines the word
solution.explanation: After the colon, the passage explains the problem: too many visitors in the same few weeks and the same few places. That is the concentration of tourism in time and space.
steps: Read after the colon: 'same few weeks', 'same few places'
Crowding in time and place = concentration
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Absence' contradicts the crowds. 'Cost' and 'taxation' are not what the colon goes on to describe.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'more ___ to landslides' after unplanned construction
solution.explanation: Building hotels on steep slopes weakens them, so towns become more vulnerable (exposed) to landslides. The next clause about worsened damage confirms the negative effect.
steps: Unplanned construction on slopes is harmful
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Immune' and 'resistant' reverse the effect of unplanned building. 'Indifferent to landslides' describes an attitude, which a town cannot have.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'a slow decline in which ...' requires a word of gradual damage
solution.explanation: The alternative to limits is 'a slow decline', in which the beauty that draws tourists is gradually worn away by crowds. 'Eroded' means worn away little by little and matches 'slow decline'.
steps: Frame: 'a slow decline in which the very beauty ... is ___ by their numbers'
Decline → the beauty is being lost
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Sustained', 'magnified' and 'showcased' all mean the beauty is kept or increased, which contradicts 'a slow decline' and the irony in 'the very beauty that draws tourists'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (1) may be wrongly used: 'The interest rate printed on the deposit receipt, however, can be misleading'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: 'however' and the next sentence show the bold word is right
solution.explanation: The printed rate 'can be misleading' because, as the next sentence says, what matters is the real rate after inflation. A saver who sees only the nominal rate is misled. The word is correct as it stands.
steps: 'however' contrasts the simple deposit with a hidden catch
Next sentence: nominal rate ≠ real rate
So the printed rate can mislead: no replacement needed
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Accurate', 'reassuring' and 'transparent' remove the contrast signalled by 'however' and contradict the passage's point that the printed rate hides the effect of inflation.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (2) may be wrongly used: 'if inflation falls above the deposit rate, the saver is in effect becoming poorer every year'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: meaning and collocation ('rise above')
solution.explanation: The saver becomes poorer when inflation goes higher than the deposit rate. Inflation 'rises above' the deposit rate; 'falls above' is self-contradictory.
steps: Condition for becoming poorer: inflation > deposit rate
Movement upward past a level: 'rises above'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Drops' repeats the error of 'falls'. 'Rising' is a participle and cannot be the main verb of the 'if' clause. 'Falls' is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (3) may be wrongly used: 'they face an uncomfortable choice: accept a gain in their real income or move their savings into riskier assets'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: an 'uncomfortable choice' must involve a loss
solution.explanation: When inflation is above deposit rates, savers relying on interest lose purchasing power. Their uncomfortable choice is to accept a decline in real income or take on risk. 'Gain' makes the choice comfortable, so it is wrong.
steps: Context: inflation high, deposit rates lag behind → real income falls
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Rise' and 'boost' repeat the error of 'gain'. 'Gain' itself is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (4) may be wrongly used: 'the mis-selling of complex products tends to rise when real rates are generous'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: link the effect back to its cause
solution.explanation: Savers move into risky products when deposits fail to beat inflation, i.e. when real rates are low. So mis-selling rises when real rates are low, not 'generous'.
steps: Cause of risk-taking in this paragraph: deposits lag behind inflation
That means real rates are low
solution.why_others_wrong: 'High' and 'attractive' repeat the error: with good real returns, savers would have no reason to chase risk. 'Generous' is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Both the branch manager (A) / as well as the cashier (B) / attended the training session. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Both' pairs with 'and', not 'as well as'
solution.explanation: The correlative is 'both ... and': 'Both the branch manager and the cashier attended the training session.' 'Both ... as well as' is incorrect.
steps: Spot the correlative opener 'Both' in part A
'as well as' → 'and': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct subject opener and part C has a correct past-tense verb with its object. Since B has an error, 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: as well as the cashier

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
We discussed about (A) / the new crop loan scheme (B) / at yesterday's meeting. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Discuss' is a transitive verb and takes a direct object (no 'about')
solution.explanation: One 'discusses something', not 'discusses about something'. The correct form is 'We discussed the new crop loan scheme at yesterday's meeting.'
steps: Check the verb in part A: 'discussed'
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B is a correct noun phrase and part C a correct time phrase. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
This year the bank has recruited (A) / less officers than (B) / it did last year. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: This year the bank has recruited

solution.concept: 'Fewer' with countable plural nouns; 'less' with uncountable nouns
solution.explanation: 'Officers' can be counted, so the sentence needs 'fewer officers than it did last year'. 'Less' is used with uncountable nouns such as 'less money'.
steps: 'less officers' → 'fewer officers': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A uses the present perfect correctly with 'This year' (a period not yet over). Part C correctly uses 'did' to stand for 'recruited'. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The agent who cheated (A) / the villagers has been arrested, (B) / and the police has filed a case. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: and the police has filed a case.

solution.concept: 'Police' is a plural noun and takes a plural verb
solution.explanation: 'Police' is always treated as plural: 'the police have filed a case'. The singular 'has' is wrong.
steps: Part B: 'The agent ... has been arrested': singular subject, singular verb, correct
Part C: subject 'the police' is plural
'has filed' → 'have filed': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A correctly uses 'who' for a person. In part B, 'has' agrees with 'The agent', not with 'villagers'. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: and the police has filed a case.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Would you mind waiting (A) / for a few minutes while (B) / I check your account details? (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Mind' takes a gerund; 'while' + present simple for a simultaneous action
solution.explanation: The sentence is correct. 'Would you mind' is followed by the gerund 'waiting', 'for a few minutes' is a correct duration phrase, and 'while I check' correctly uses the present simple for an action happening at the same time.
steps: Part B: 'for' + period of time; 'while' as a linker: correct
Part C: present simple after 'while': correct
solution.why_others_wrong: Each of parts A, B and C is correct, as shown in the steps, so none of them is the answer.

steps: 'Many a' is always followed by a singular noun and a singular verb

The officer whom we thought (A) / was responsible for the delay (B) / turned out to be on leave that week. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: turned out to be on leave that week.

solution.concept: Who vs whom: the pronoun is the subject of 'was', so it must be 'who'
solution.explanation: Remove the inserted 'we thought': 'The officer who was responsible for the delay'. The pronoun is the subject of 'was', so 'who' is required: 'The officer who we thought was responsible ...'.
steps: The pronoun becomes the subject of 'was responsible'
Subject form: 'who', not 'whom': error in part A

The more carefully a bank checks (A) / a borrower's credit history, (B) / lesser is the chance of a default. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The more carefully a bank checks
lesser is the chance of a default.

solution.explanation: A sentence beginning 'The more ...' must continue with 'the' + comparative in the second half: 'the smaller the chance of a default' (or 'the less likely a default'). 'Lesser is the chance' breaks the pattern, and 'lesser' is not used for amounts or chances in this way.
steps: Part A opens the pattern 'The more ...'
Second half must be 'the + comparative': 'the smaller the chance'
'lesser is the chance' is wrong: error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A correctly uses 'The more carefully' and part B is a correct object phrase. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: lesser is the chance of a default.

or the finance head has signed it yet.

solution.concept: Correlative pair: 'neither ... nor'
solution.explanation: 'Neither' must be paired with 'nor': 'neither the chief executive nor the finance head has signed it yet'. The singular verb 'has' is correct because both subjects are singular.
steps: 'or' → 'nor': error in part C (the verb 'has' is fine)
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A uses a correct present perfect. Part B correctly opens the correlative. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
