Not until the audit was completed (A) / did the board realise (B) / how large the losses were. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: Not until the audit was completed

solution.concept: Inversion after a negative opening ('Not until ...' + auxiliary + subject); embedded question in statement order
solution.explanation: The sentence is correct. A sentence starting with 'Not until ...' inverts the main clause ('did the board realise'), and the embedded question 'how large the losses were' correctly keeps statement word order.
steps: Part A: 'Not until' + a complete time clause: correct
Part B: inversion 'did the board realise': correct after 'Not until'
Part C: embedded question in statement order ('the losses were'): correct
solution.why_others_wrong: A is a correct time clause, B shows the required inversion, and C correctly avoids question order ('how large were the losses') inside a statement. None of them contains an error.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
Most young customers **prefer using the app than visiting** the branch.

options.text: prefer to using the app than visiting
prefer using the app to visiting
are preferring using the app than visiting

solution.concept: 'Prefer A to B' (not 'prefer A than B')
solution.explanation: With 'prefer' + gerund, the thing preferred is compared using 'to': 'prefer using the app to visiting the branch'.
steps: The comparison word after 'prefer' is 'to', not 'than'
Keep both gerunds parallel: using ... visiting
solution.why_others_wrong: A puts 'to' in the wrong place and keeps 'than'. C keeps 'than' and wrongly uses 'prefer' in the continuous form for a general preference. The original uses 'than', so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: prefer using the app to visiting

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
The new clerk **cannot cope up with** the pressure of the month-end closing.

solution.concept: 'Cope with' (no 'up')
solution.explanation: The verb is 'cope with': 'The new clerk cannot cope with the pressure.' 'Cope up with' is a common error.
solution.why_others_wrong: B keeps 'up' and uses the wrong preposition. C keeps 'up' and uses '-ing' after 'cannot'. The original is wrong, so 'No improvement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
It is two years **since he has joined** the bank as a probationary officer.

solution.concept: 'It is + period + since + simple past'
solution.explanation: In the pattern 'It is two years since ...', the 'since' clause names a past event and takes the simple past: 'It is two years since he joined the bank.'
steps: The past event takes the simple past
solution.why_others_wrong: A uses the past perfect, which needs another past reference point. C replaces 'since' with 'for', which cannot introduce a clause here. The present perfect in the original is wrong, so 'No improvement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
Looking at the long queue today, I wish I **had applied** for the online account last year.

solution.concept: 'Wish' + past perfect for a regret about the past
solution.explanation: The regret concerns a past action ('last year'), so 'wish' takes the past perfect: 'I wish I had applied ...'. The sentence is already correct.
steps: Time of the wished-for action: last year (past)
Regret about the past: wish + past perfect
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Applied' (simple past) after 'wish' expresses a present wish, which clashes with 'last year'. 'Have applied' and 'would apply' are not used after 'wish' for a past regret.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
She **has been knowing** the branch manager for more than ten years.

solution.concept: Stative verbs ('know') are not used in continuous forms
solution.explanation: 'Know' describes a state, not an action, so it does not take the continuous. With 'for more than ten years', the present perfect is needed: 'She has known the branch manager for more than ten years.'
steps: 'know' is a stative verb: no -ing form
Duration up to now ('for ... years') → present perfect
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Is knowing' is a continuous form of a stative verb. 'Knows' (present simple) does not go with 'for more than ten years'. The original is wrong, so 'No improvement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
It is getting late, so we **had better to leave** before the roads are flooded.

solution.concept: 'Had better' + bare infinitive (no 'to')
solution.explanation: 'Had better' is followed by the base form of the verb without 'to': 'we had better leave before the roads are flooded'.
solution.why_others_wrong: A adds 'to' and an -ing form. 'Would better' is not an English expression. The original wrongly uses 'to', so 'No improvement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
The auditor **suggested him to check** all the vouchers again.

solution.concept: 'Suggest' does not take object + to-infinitive; use a 'that' clause
solution.explanation: 'Suggest' cannot be followed by 'him to check'. The standard pattern is a 'that' clause: 'The auditor suggested that he should check all the vouchers again.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Suggested him for checking' and 'suggested to him to check' are both unidiomatic. The original is wrong, so 'No improvement required' does not apply.
solution.final_answer: Option B: suggested that he should check

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
She is one of those officers **who has always refused** to cut corners.

solution.concept: In 'one of those + plural noun + who', the relative pronoun refers to the plural noun
solution.explanation: The relative clause describes 'those officers' (the group that refuses to cut corners); she is one of them. 'Who' therefore takes a plural verb: 'one of those officers who have always refused'.
solution.why_others_wrong: B uses 'which' for people and keeps the singular verb. C keeps the singular verb and changes the meaning to an ongoing action. The original is wrong, so 'No improvement required' does not apply.
solution.final_answer: Option A: who have always refused

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
**Had the bank informed earlier**, it could have blocked the stolen card at once.

options.text: If the bank had informed earlier
Had the bank being informed earlier
Had the bank been informed earlier

solution.concept: Inverted third conditional with a passive verb ('Had + subject + been + V3')
solution.explanation: The bank did not inform anyone; it should have been informed. The passive is needed, and the inverted conditional is 'Had + subject + been + past participle': 'Had the bank been informed earlier, it could have blocked the card.'
steps: Who informs whom? The customer informs the bank, so the bank is the receiver: passive
Inverted third conditional: Had + subject + past participle
solution.why_others_wrong: A keeps the active 'had informed', which leaves 'inform' without an object and wrongly makes the bank the informer. B uses 'being' instead of 'been'. The original is wrong, so 'No improvement required' does not apply.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Had the bank been informed earlier

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
The manager **called off** the review meeting because half the members were absent.

solution.concept: Phrasal verbs with 'call': call off = cancel
solution.explanation: Half the members were absent, so the meeting was cancelled. 'Called off' means cancelled, which fits exactly.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Called on' means visited or asked to speak. 'Called for' means demanded. 'Called in' means summoned someone. None fits a meeting cancelled for lack of members.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
The board **turned off** the expansion proposal because it was too costly.

solution.concept: Phrasal verbs with 'turn': turn down = reject
solution.explanation: A proposal that is too costly is rejected. 'Turn down' means reject; 'turn off' means switch off (a device).
steps: Context: the proposal is too costly
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Turned up' means appeared or increased. 'Turned over' means handed over or flipped. The original 'turned off' is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
**In lieu of** the festival, the branch will remain closed on Thursday.

solution.concept: 'In lieu of' = instead of; 'on account of' = because of
solution.explanation: The festival is the reason the branch will close, so a phrase meaning 'because of' is needed: 'On account of the festival, the branch will remain closed.' 'In lieu of' means 'instead of', which makes no sense here.
steps: Relation between festival and closure: cause
solution.why_others_wrong: 'In spite of' expresses contrast, not cause. 'In place of' means the same as 'in lieu of'. The original is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
The minister's claim **was on contrary to** the data released by her own ministry.

solution.concept: Fixed expression: 'run contrary to' / 'be contrary to'
solution.explanation: The idiom is 'contrary to' with no 'on': 'The minister's claim ran contrary to the data.' 'Ran contrary to' means went against.
solution.why_others_wrong: A uses the wrong preposition 'with'. B uses the plural 'were' with the singular subject 'claim'. The original 'was on contrary to' is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
Most retired depositors **are averse from** taking risks with their savings.

solution.concept: 'Averse to' = opposed to, unwilling; 'adverse' = harmful, unfavourable
solution.explanation: People who dislike risk are 'averse to' it: 'Most retired depositors are averse to taking risks.' The preposition is 'to'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Adverse' means harmful ('adverse effects') and does not describe a person's attitude. 'Averse for' uses the wrong preposition. The original is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: A customer is comparing a bank's new mobile app with its old one. Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?

options.text: This app is more faster than the old one.
This app is faster than the old one.
This app is most faster than the old one.
This app is fastest than the old one.

solution.concept: Comparative degree: one-syllable adjectives add -er; no 'more' or 'most' with it
solution.explanation: Comparing two things needs the comparative 'faster', and 'than' follows the comparative. 'More faster' is a double comparative.
solution.why_others_wrong: A and C add 'more' or 'most' to a form that is already comparative. D uses the superlative with 'than'.
solution.final_answer: Option B: This app is faster than the old one.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Four remarks were overheard at a branch counter. Which of the following sentences is grammatically INCORRECT?

options.text: I don't know anything about the new scheme.
She hardly ever visits the branch.
He can't hardly read the small print on the form.
We have never missed a payment.

solution.concept: Double negatives: 'hardly' is already negative
solution.explanation: 'Hardly' has a negative meaning, so it cannot be combined with 'can't'. The correct form is 'He can hardly read the small print.'
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and D each contain only one negative and are correct.
solution.final_answer: Option C: He can't hardly read the small print on the form.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following requests from a colleague is grammatically correct?

options.text: Please keep this matter between you and I.
Please keep this matter between you and myself.
Please keep this matter between I and you.
Please keep this matter between you and me.

solution.concept: A pronoun after a preposition takes the object form
solution.explanation: 'Between' is a preposition, so the pronouns after it must be object forms: 'between you and me'.
solution.why_others_wrong: A and C use the subject pronoun 'I' after a preposition. B uses the reflexive 'myself', which needs a matching subject ('I ... myself') and is wrong here.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Please keep this matter between you and me.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?

options.text: The clerk admitted making an error in the ledger.
The clerk admitted to make an error in the ledger.
The clerk admitted of making an error in the ledger.
The clerk admitted to have made an error in the ledger.

solution.concept: 'Admit' + gerund (or 'admit to' + gerund); never 'admit' + to-infinitive
solution.explanation: 'Admit' is followed by a gerund: 'admitted making an error'. ('Admitted to making' is also correct, but it is not among the options.)
steps: B and D: 'to' + infinitive after 'admit': wrong
C: 'admit of' means 'allow' and does not fit
solution.why_others_wrong: B and D use a to-infinitive after 'admit', which is incorrect. C uses 'admit of', which means 'leave room for' ('The facts admit of no doubt') and cannot be used for confessing.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The clerk admitted making an error in the ledger.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically INCORRECT?

options.text: The scheme will benefit farmers as well as traders.
The manager made him to sign the register again.
She is the more capable of the two officers.

solution.concept: Causative 'make' + object + bare infinitive (in the active voice)
solution.explanation: In the active voice, 'make someone do something' takes the base form without 'to': 'The manager made him sign the register again.'
steps: A: 'as well as' joins two nouns: correct
C: 'made him to sign': 'to' must be dropped, incorrect
D: comparative 'the more capable of the two': correct
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and D are correct. D in particular rightly uses the comparative for two people.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The manager made him to sign the register again.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?

options.text: The files have laid untouched on the shelf for months.
The files have lain untouched on the shelf for months.
The files have lied untouched on the shelf for months.
The files have layed untouched on the shelf for months.

solution.concept: Lie (rest) – lay – lain vs lay (put) – laid – laid
solution.explanation: The files are resting, so the verb is intransitive 'lie', whose past participle is 'lain': 'The files have lain untouched for months.'
steps: Are the files resting or putting something? Resting → 'lie'
solution.why_others_wrong: A uses 'laid', the participle of 'lay' (to put), which needs an object. C uses 'lied', which belongs to 'lie' meaning to tell an untruth. D 'layed' is not a standard form.
solution.final_answer: Option B: The files have lain untouched on the shelf for months.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically INCORRECT?

options.text: Were the bank to raise its rates, many borrowers would protest.
Not only did sales fall, but costs also rose.
Having been warned twice, the clerk was finally suspended.
Write down the reference number lest you should not forget it.

solution.concept: 'Lest' already means 'so that ... not'; it is not followed by another negative
solution.explanation: 'Lest' carries the negative meaning, so 'lest you should not forget' is a double negative and says the opposite of what is meant. The correct form is 'lest you should forget it' (or 'lest you forget it').
steps: A: inverted conditional 'Were the bank to ...': correct
B: 'Not only did ... but ... also': correct
C: participle phrase whose doer is 'the clerk', the subject: correct
D: 'lest ... should not': double negative, incorrect
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are correct. C is not a dangling modifier: the clerk is the one who was warned.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Write down the reference number lest you should not forget it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) With the loan, she bought a second-hand sewing machine.
(B) Meena had always wanted to start a tailoring business from her home.
(C) Within a year, she had repaid the loan and hired two assistants.
(D) But she did not have enough money to buy a machine.
(E) So she approached her self-help group for a small loan.

solution.concept: Para jumble: named opener, then problem, solution, action and result
solution.explanation: B introduces Meena and her wish. D gives the problem ('But ... not enough money'). E gives her response ('So she approached ...'). A uses 'the loan', so it follows E. C ('Within a year') closes the story.
steps: Opener: B (names Meena; the others use 'she')
E → A: 'the loan' refers to E's loan; C last: BDEAC
solution.why_others_wrong: BEDAC has her seek a loan before the money problem is stated. DBEAC opens with 'But she' before Meena is named. BDAEC has her use 'the loan' before asking for it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) The town's weekly market is held every Sunday near the bus stand.
(P) Farmers from nearby villages arrive early with vegetables, grain and milk.
(Q) By eight in the morning, the ground is crowded with buyers.
(R) By noon, most of the stock has been sold and the stalls begin to close.
(S) The farmers then use their earnings to buy seeds and household goods before heading home.

solution.concept: Fixed opener; follow the time sequence (early → eight o'clock → noon → then)
solution.explanation: The sentences follow the market day: farmers arrive early (P), buyers crowd in by eight (Q), stock is sold by noon (R), and the farmers then spend their earnings (S).
steps: S: 'then use their earnings' after selling: PQRS
solution.why_others_wrong: PRQS puts noon before eight o'clock. QPRS has buyers crowding the ground before the sellers arrive. PQSR has farmers spending earnings before the stock is sold.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) Last year, the school installed solar panels on its roof with help from the panchayat.
(B) The money saved on electricity bills is now being used to buy books for the library.
(C) A village school often lost power for hours during the afternoon.
(D) The panels now supply most of the school's electricity during the day.
(E) As a result, teachers found it hard to use the computers donated by a local firm.

solution.concept: Para jumble: problem → its effect → solution → result → further benefit
solution.explanation: C introduces the school and the power cuts. E states the effect ('As a result'). A gives the solution (solar panels). D describes what 'the panels' now do. B mentions money saved, which follows from D.
steps: C → E: 'As a result' follows the power cuts
A introduces the panels; D refers to 'The panels'
solution.why_others_wrong: CAEDB puts the solution before the effect of the problem, so 'As a result' follows the solar panels. ECADB opens with 'As a result'. CEABD mentions savings before saying the panels supply the electricity.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) Earlier, passengers had to stand in long queues at the station to buy a railway ticket.
(P) They are still used by passengers who are not comfortable with smartphones.
(Q) Later, computerised reservation counters made it possible to book a ticket for any train from any major station.
(R) Even so, the counters have not disappeared completely.
(S) Today, most tickets are booked online in a few minutes.

solution.concept: Time markers (Earlier → Later → Today) and the pronoun 'They'
solution.explanation: The paragraph moves through time: queues earlier (1), computerised counters later (Q), online booking today (S). R ('Even so') contrasts with S, and P ('They') refers to 'the counters' in R.
steps: R: 'Even so' contrasts with online booking
P: 'They' = the counters in R: QSRP
solution.why_others_wrong: SQRP puts 'Today' before 'Later'. QRSP says counters have not disappeared before online booking is mentioned. QSPR makes 'They' refer to tickets.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) Manufacturers argue that unauthorised repairs could compromise safety and void warranties.
(B) Campaigners, however, say such claims are often used to protect profitable service monopolies.
(C) When a smartphone or a tractor breaks down, its owner is often forced to go back to the company that made it.
(D) This is because spare parts, manuals and diagnostic software are not available to independent repairers.
(E) A growing 'right to repair' movement wants these restrictions removed.

solution.concept: Para jumble: situation → cause ('This is because') → movement → objection → reply
solution.explanation: C states the situation. D explains it ('This is because ...'). E introduces the movement against 'these restrictions'. A gives the manufacturers' objection, and B replies to 'such claims' with 'however'.
steps: E: 'these restrictions' = the restrictions in D
solution.why_others_wrong: CEDAB mentions 'these restrictions' before they are described. ECDAB opens with 'these restrictions'. CDAEB puts the manufacturers' reply before the movement they are replying to.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) Hospitals in many cities are turning to telemedicine to reach patients in remote areas.
(P) A doctor in the city can then examine the reports, speak to the patient on a video call and prescribe treatment.
(Q) Under this arrangement, a health worker at a village centre records the patient's symptoms and basic test results.
(R) This saves the patient a long and expensive journey.
(S) It cannot, however, replace a physical examination when a serious condition is suspected.

solution.concept: Process order ('then') and a final limitation ('however')
solution.explanation: Q explains the arrangement (a health worker records details). P follows with 'then' (the doctor examines the reports). R gives the benefit, and S ends with the limitation.
steps: Q → P: the doctor examines the reports Q mentions
solution.why_others_wrong: PQRS has the doctor examine 'the reports' before they are recorded. QRPS states the benefit before describing the consultation. QPSR gives the limitation before the benefit, leaving 'This saves ...' with an unclear referent.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) Instead, they reduce the quantity in each pack while keeping the price unchanged.
(B) When the cost of raw materials rises, companies selling packaged goods face a dilemma.
(C) Economists call this practice 'shrinkflation'.
(D) Raising prices openly risks driving away customers who watch price tags closely.
(E) Shrinkflation often goes unnoticed, because shoppers check prices far more often than pack sizes.

solution.concept: Para jumble: dilemma → rejected option → 'Instead' → name → consequence of the named practice
solution.explanation: B states the dilemma. D gives the rejected option (raising prices). A begins 'Instead', so it follows D. C names 'this practice' (A's). E uses the term 'Shrinkflation', so it must come after C defines it.
steps: D → A: 'Instead' needs an option to replace
E uses the name, so it comes after C: BDACE
solution.why_others_wrong: BADCE puts 'Instead' before the option it replaces. BDAEC uses the term 'Shrinkflation' before it is introduced. DBACE begins with the rejected option before the dilemma is set up.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) For most of history, a trader's reputation in the marketplace travelled by word of mouth.
(P) That very scale, however, has made ratings an attractive target for manipulation.
(Q) Online ratings promised to scale up this ancient mechanism to millions of buyers and sellers.
(R) Fake reviews, bought in bulk, can now lift an indifferent product above an excellent one.
(S) A trader who cheated one customer would soon find that others had heard about it.

solution.concept: Fixed opener; 'this ancient mechanism' and 'That very scale' as links
solution.explanation: S illustrates word of mouth from (1). Q calls it 'this ancient mechanism' and introduces online ratings. P ('That very scale') refers to Q's 'millions'. R gives the result of the manipulation in P.
steps: (1) → S: an example of word of mouth
S → Q: 'this ancient mechanism' = word of mouth
Q → P: 'That very scale' = millions of buyers and sellers
P → R: manipulation → fake reviews: SQPR
solution.why_others_wrong: QSPR moves to online ratings and then back to the old marketplace example. SPQR mentions 'That very scale' before any scale is described. SQRP gives the fake-review result before the manipulation that explains it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) Supporters point to trials in which output held steady even as working hours fell.
(B) Sceptics reply that the firms in these trials volunteered and were therefore likely to succeed.
(C) The idea of a four-day working week has moved from the fringes to mainstream debate.
(D) Whether such results would hold across an entire economy therefore remains an open question.
(E) Employees in these trials also reported less stress and fewer sick days.

solution.concept: Para jumble: topic → supporters' evidence → added evidence → objection → conclusion
solution.explanation: C introduces the debate. A gives the supporters' evidence (trials). E adds to it ('also', 'these trials'). B gives the sceptics' reply. D draws the conclusion ('therefore') from the doubt raised in B.
steps: A introduces 'trials'; E ('these trials ... also') extends A
B: sceptics' reply to the evidence
solution.why_others_wrong: CABED separates E from the supporters' evidence and puts it after the sceptics' reply. CEABD mentions 'these trials' before any trial is introduced. CAEDB draws the conclusion before the doubt that justifies it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) A city's informal settlements are often described only in terms of what they lack.
(P) Yet many of them are also dense networks of small enterprises, from tailoring units to recycling workshops.
(Q) Treating these areas solely as problems to be cleared can therefore destroy livelihoods along with shacks.
(R) By contrast, upgrading them in place, with water, drainage and secure tenure, tends to preserve those networks.
(S) Residents typically live close to where they work, often in the same building.

solution.concept: Fixed opener; 'Yet' contrasts with (1), 'therefore' and 'By contrast' order the argument
solution.explanation: P contrasts with (1) ('Yet ... also'). S adds detail about those enterprises (people live where they work). Q draws the consequence ('therefore') of clearing such areas. R offers the alternative ('By contrast').
steps: (1) → P: 'Yet' answers 'only in terms of what they lack'
P → S: detail about the work networks
Q: 'therefore' follows from P and S
solution.why_others_wrong: PQSR draws the conclusion (Q) before S finishes the evidence. SPQR describes residents' work before the enterprises are introduced. RPSQ offers the contrast before there is anything to contrast with.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following parts (P), (Q), (R) and (S) to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
(P) to all account holders
(Q) the bank sent
(R) about the new service charges
(S) a text message

solution.concept: Subject + verb + direct object, then the prepositional phrases
solution.explanation: 'The bank sent a text message to all account holders about the new service charges.' The verb 'sent' (Q) is followed by its object 'a text message' (S), then 'to whom' (P) and 'about what' (R).
steps: Direct object follows the verb: S
Then the recipients (P) and the topic (R): QSPR
solution.why_others_wrong: SQPR places the object before the subject and verb. QPRS separates 'sent' from its object and leaves 'a text message' dangling at the end. PQSR begins with a prepositional phrase that cannot open this sentence.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following parts (P), (Q), (R) and (S) to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
(P) the farmers who had
(Q) lost their crops to the floods
(R) were given
(S) interest-free loans by the cooperative

solution.concept: Relative clause completed before the main verb; passive verb + object + agent
solution.explanation: 'The farmers who had lost their crops to the floods were given interest-free loans by the cooperative.' The relative clause (P + Q) must be complete before the main verb 'were given' (R).
steps: P ends with 'who had', which needs a past participle: Q ('lost ...')
Then the main verb R ('were given')
Then what was given and by whom: S: PQRS
solution.why_others_wrong: PRQS gives 'who had were given', which is ungrammatical. QPRS cannot start with 'lost'. PQSR puts the object before the verb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The new mobile app makes it ______ for customers to check their balance at any time.

solution.concept: 'Make it + adjective + for + person + to-infinitive'
solution.explanation: In 'makes it ___ for customers to check', 'it' is the object and the blank is its complement, which must be an adjective: 'makes it easy'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Easily' is an adverb, and 'ease' and 'easiness' are nouns; none can be the complement of 'it' in this pattern.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
The bank ______ the customer's request and ______ a duplicate passbook within a week.

solution.concept: Double blank: both words must agree in meaning
solution.explanation: The sentence describes a request being met: the bank accepted the request and issued a duplicate passbook.
steps: The 'and' joins two actions in the same direction
solution.why_others_wrong: A and D pair a refusal or neglect of the request with a helpful action, which is contradictory. C pairs accepting the request with cancelling the passbook, which defeats the request.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
Despite repeated reminders from the branch, the borrower remained ______ and made no effort to repay the loan.

solution.concept: Single blank: 'Despite' signals that the borrower did not respond
solution.explanation: Repeated reminders produced no response, so the borrower was unconcerned: 'indifferent'.
steps: 'Despite repeated reminders' → the reminders had no effect
'made no effort' confirms lack of concern
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Prompt' and 'punctual' contradict 'made no effort to repay'. 'Grateful' does not fit the lack of response.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
The audit ______ several lapses in record-keeping, but the inspector found no ______ of fraud.

solution.concept: Double blank: 'but' contrasts lapses with the absence of fraud
solution.explanation: An audit reveals (brings to light) lapses. 'But' introduces a contrast: there were lapses, yet no evidence of fraud.
steps: Blank 1: what an audit does with lapses → 'revealed'
solution.why_others_wrong: A: an audit does not conceal lapses. B: 'found no absence of fraud' would mean fraud was present, which clashes with 'but'. C: an audit does not praise lapses.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the phrase that best fills the blank.
The road project was abandoned ______ funds, and the half-built bridge still stands unused.

solution.concept: Fixed phrase: 'for want of' = because of a lack of
solution.explanation: The project stopped because there was not enough money. The fixed phrase is 'for want of funds'.
steps: Meaning needed: because of a lack of
solution.why_others_wrong: 'In want for', 'by want of' and 'on want of' are not English phrases.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
The regulator's response was ______: instead of addressing the root cause of the losses, it merely ______ the symptoms.

solution.concept: Double blank: the colon explains the first word; 'merely' limits the second
solution.explanation: The colon explains the response: it dealt only with symptoms, not causes. That is a 'superficial' response that 'merely treated the symptoms'.
steps: After the colon: root cause ignored, symptoms handled → superficial
'merely ___ the symptoms' → it did deal with them, but only them → 'treated'
solution.why_others_wrong: A: 'thorough' contradicts ignoring the root cause. C: 'merely ignored the symptoms' makes no sense; if it ignored both causes and symptoms, 'merely' has no point. D: 'cured' is too strong for a response criticised as inadequate, and 'delayed' is not what the colon explains.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
His explanation for the missing funds was so ______ that even his closest colleagues found it hard to believe.

solution.concept: Single blank: 'so ... that' result clause
solution.explanation: The result is that even his friends could not believe it, so the explanation must have been unlikely or improbable: 'far-fetched'.
steps: Result: 'even his closest colleagues found it hard to believe'
Cause must be a quality that makes something unbelievable
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Cogent' (convincing), 'lucid' (clear) and 'candid' (frank) are qualities that would make an explanation easier to believe, not harder.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'affect' used correctly?

options.text: The strike will effect the bank's operations in the district.
The rate cut had no affect on deposits.
The new rule will affect all current account holders.
The affect of the rate cut was felt within a month.

solution.concept: Affect (verb: to influence) vs effect (noun: result)
solution.explanation: 'Affect' is normally a verb meaning 'to influence'. In C it is used as a verb: 'The new rule will affect all current account holders.'
steps: A uses 'effect' as a verb meaning 'influence': wrong (it should be 'affect')
B and D use 'affect' as a noun meaning 'result': wrong (it should be 'effect')
C uses 'affect' as a verb: correct
solution.why_others_wrong: A should read 'will affect the bank's operations'. B should read 'no effect on deposits'. D should read 'The effect of the rate cut'.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The new rule will affect all current account holders.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
In the sentence below, four words are in bold. Two of them may need to be interchanged to make the sentence meaningful. Choose the correct swap; if no swap is needed, choose 'No swap required'.
The **(A) deposit** asked the cashier to **(B) customer** the cheque **(C) into** his savings **(D) account**.

solution.concept: Word swap: check each bold word in its slot
solution.explanation: A customer asks a cashier to deposit a cheque. Swapping A and B gives: 'The customer asked the cashier to deposit the cheque into his savings account.'
steps: 'The deposit asked the cashier' makes no sense
'to customer the cheque' makes no sense
Swap A and B; 'into' and 'account' are already correct
solution.why_others_wrong: A-C gives 'The into asked the cashier'. B-D gives 'to account the cheque into his savings customer'. The sentence clearly needs a swap.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'discreet' used correctly?

options.text: The data were divided into four discreet categories.
Each instalment is a discreet payment recorded separately.
The two accounts are kept in discreet ledgers.
The manager made a discreet inquiry about the borrower's other debts.

solution.concept: Discreet (careful, tactful, not drawing attention) vs discrete (separate, distinct)
solution.explanation: 'Discreet' means careful and tactful so as not to cause embarrassment. A quiet, tactful inquiry about someone's debts is a 'discreet inquiry'.
steps: A, B and C all mean 'separate' or 'distinct': they need 'discrete'
D means a careful, tactful inquiry: 'discreet' is correct
solution.why_others_wrong: A ('discrete categories'), B ('a discrete payment') and C ('discrete ledgers') need 'discrete', meaning separate.
solution.final_answer: Option D: The manager made a discreet inquiry about the borrower's other debts.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'flout' used correctly?

options.text: The company was fined for flouting the safety rules at its plant.
He liked to flout his new car in front of his neighbours.
The winners flouted their trophy at the parade.
She flouted her knowledge of tax law at every meeting.

solution.concept: Flout (openly disobey a rule) vs flaunt (show off)
solution.explanation: 'Flout' means to break or openly disregard a rule. A company fined for ignoring safety rules has 'flouted' them.
steps: B, C and D describe showing off → they need 'flaunt'
solution.why_others_wrong: B ('flaunt his new car'), C ('flaunted their trophy') and D ('flaunted her knowledge') confuse 'flout' with 'flaunt'.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The company was fined for flouting the safety rules at its plant.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
In the sentence below, four words are in bold. Two of them may need to be interchanged to make the sentence meaningful. Choose the correct swap; if no swap is needed, choose 'No swap required'.
The **(A) committee** decided to keep the policy rate unchanged because **(B) target** had not yet **(C) eased** to its **(D) inflation**.

solution.concept: Word swap: subject–object logic in the 'because' clause
solution.explanation: It is inflation that eases towards a target, not a target that eases to its inflation. Swapping B and D gives: '... because inflation had not yet eased to its target.'
steps: 'committee decided' and 'eased' are correct in place
'target had not yet eased to its inflation' reverses the logic
Swap B and D: 'inflation had not yet eased to its target'
solution.why_others_wrong: A-B gives 'The target decided', which is meaningless. A-D gives 'The inflation decided ... to its committee'. The sentence needs a swap, so 'No swap required' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'lapsed' as used in the sentence:
'His insurance policy lapsed because he forgot to pay the premium for three months.'

solution.concept: Lapse (of a policy or right) = come to an end through neglect
solution.explanation: A policy whose premium is not paid stops being in force. 'Lapsed' means it ceased to be valid.
steps: Cause: premium unpaid for three months
Result for a policy: it ends
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Was renewed' and 'doubled in value' are the opposite of what non-payment causes. 'Was transferred' has no link with missing premiums.
solution.final_answer: Option B: ceased to be valid

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs consists of words that are SIMILAR in meaning?

solution.concept: Word pairs: identify synonyms and antonyms
solution.explanation: 'Ample' and 'plentiful' both mean more than enough. The other three pairs are opposites.
solution.why_others_wrong: B, C and D are pairs of opposites, not synonyms.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'lax' as used in the sentence:
'The inspection report was scathing about the branch's lax control over cash in the vault.'

solution.concept: Lax = not strict or careful enough
solution.explanation: A 'scathing' (severely critical) report criticises weak control. 'Lax control' is loose, careless control.
steps: So the control must have been poor
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Strict' is the opposite and would not draw harsh criticism. 'Costly' and 'secret' do not describe a weakness in control.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs consists of words that are OPPOSITE in meaning?

solution.concept: Advanced vocabulary: synonym and antonym pairs
solution.explanation: 'Parsimonious' means extremely unwilling to spend money; 'lavish' means spending generously. They are opposites. The other pairs are synonyms.
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are pairs of synonyms, not opposites.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The branch manager sent a **brief** reply to the customer's long letter of complaint.

solution.concept: Brief = short
solution.explanation: A 'brief' reply is a short one; the contrast with the customer's 'long letter' confirms the meaning.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Detailed' is close to the opposite. 'Rude' and 'delayed' describe tone and timing, not length.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The cashier **verified** the signature on the cheque before paying out the amount.

solution.concept: Verify = check that something is true or genuine
solution.explanation: Before paying, a cashier makes sure the signature is genuine: he checks it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Ignored' is the opposite of a precaution. 'Copied' and 'forged' describe fraud, not verification.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The minister **lauded** the bank staff for keeping branches open during the floods.

solution.concept: Laud = praise
solution.explanation: Keeping branches open during floods deserves praise; 'lauded' means praised highly.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Criticised' is the opposite. 'Ignored' and 'doubted' do not fit a reaction to commendable work.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
Customers were asked to **retain** the receipt until the amount was credited to their account.

solution.concept: Retain = keep
solution.explanation: The receipt is proof until the money is credited, so customers must keep it. 'Retain' means keep.
steps: Context: receipt needed until the credit appears
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Discard' is the opposite. 'Sign' and 'copy' are different actions and do not mean holding on to something.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The new chairman is known for his **pragmatic** approach: he prefers workable solutions to grand theories.

solution.concept: Pragmatic = dealing with things in a practical, realistic way
solution.explanation: The sentence explains the word: he prefers workable solutions to grand theories. That is a practical approach.
steps: Explanation after the colon: workable solutions over theories
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Idealistic' is nearly the opposite (theories over practice). 'Careless' and 'cautious' are not suggested by the explanation.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The scheme was launched with great fanfare, but its impact on rural unemployment has been **negligible**.

solution.concept: Negligible = so small as not to matter
solution.explanation: 'With great fanfare, but ...' sets up a contrast: big publicity, tiny impact. 'Negligible' means insignificant.
steps: 'but' contrasts the grand launch with the result
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Immense' and 'lasting' remove the contrast. 'Harmful' changes the meaning from small to damaging.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The board's decision to **defer** the dividend until the next quarter surprised shareholders.

solution.concept: Defer = put off to a later time
solution.explanation: 'Until the next quarter' shows the dividend is not being dropped but moved to a later date: 'postpone'.
steps: Moved to a later date = postponed
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Cancel' would not fit 'until the next quarter'. 'Increase' and 'announce' do not mean delaying.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The manager was **reluctant** to approve the loan without any collateral.

solution.concept: Reluctant = unwilling; antonym: eager
solution.explanation: 'Reluctant' means unwilling or hesitant. Its opposite is 'eager'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Unwilling' and 'hesitant' are synonyms of 'reluctant'. 'Afraid' is close in feeling, not opposite.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The company's profits have shown a **steady** rise over the last five years.

solution.concept: Steady = regular, even; antonym: erratic (irregular, unpredictable)
solution.explanation: A 'steady' rise is even and regular. The opposite is an 'erratic' pattern, irregular and unpredictable.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Constant', 'gradual' and 'regular' are all close in meaning to 'steady'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The new manager's **transparent** style of working quickly won the trust of the staff.

solution.concept: Transparent (of conduct) = open, nothing hidden; antonym: secretive
solution.explanation: A 'transparent' style is open, with nothing hidden, which is why it earned trust. The opposite is 'secretive'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Open', 'clear' and 'honest' are all similar to 'transparent' in this sense.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
Asked about the rise in bad loans, the official gave only a **vague** answer.

solution.concept: Vague = not clear or definite; antonym: precise
solution.explanation: A 'vague' answer lacks detail and clarity. The opposite is a 'precise' answer.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Unclear' is a synonym. 'Brief' and 'polite' describe length and manner, not clarity.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The chairman's **conciliatory** remarks helped ease the tension between the management and the union.

solution.concept: Conciliatory = intended to calm anger or make peace; antonym: provocative
solution.explanation: 'Conciliatory' remarks are meant to pacify, which is why they 'helped ease the tension'. The opposite is 'provocative', meaning likely to cause anger.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Soothing', 'apologetic' and 'diplomatic' are all close in meaning to 'conciliatory'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'to keep one's head above water'.

options.text: to swim well in deep water
to be very proud of oneself
to manage to survive, especially in financial difficulty
to take a very big risk

solution.concept: Idiom: keep one's head above water
solution.explanation: The idiom means to just about manage to survive a difficult situation, usually a financial one. For example, 'With sales down, the shop is barely keeping its head above water.'
steps: Image: a person struggling not to sink
Meaning: to survive, just about, in difficulty
solution.why_others_wrong: 'To swim well' takes the idiom literally. 'To be very proud' and 'to take a big risk' have no link with it.
solution.final_answer: Option C: to manage to survive, especially in financial difficulty

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the idiom in bold.
After losing its two biggest clients, the small trading firm was **on its last legs**.

solution.concept: Idiom: on its last legs = close to failure or the end
solution.explanation: Losing its two biggest clients has left the firm close to failing: 'on its last legs'.
steps: Context: the firm has lost its biggest clients
Idiom: near the end, about to fail
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Growing rapidly' contradicts the context. 'Moving office' and 'looking for a merger' are not meanings of the idiom.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the idiom in bold.
The claim that the deficit would be met without any new taxes was taken **with a pinch of salt** by most economists.

solution.concept: Idiom: take something with a pinch of salt = not believe it fully
solution.explanation: Economists were sceptical that the deficit could be met without new taxes, so they did not fully believe the claim.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'With complete trust' is the opposite. 'Open anger' and 'amusement' are reactions the idiom does not express.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the one word that can be substituted for the given group of words.
A person who lends money at very high rates of interest

solution.concept: One-word substitution: lending terms
solution.explanation: A 'usurer' lends money at excessively high interest ('usury').
solution.why_others_wrong: A 'debtor' owes money. An 'auditor' examines accounts. A 'philanthropist' gives money to good causes.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the one word that can be substituted for the given group of words.
A list of items to be discussed at a meeting

solution.concept: One-word substitution: meeting terms
solution.explanation: The 'agenda' is the list of items to be discussed at a meeting.
steps: Before the meeting: list of topics = agenda
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Minutes' are the written record of what was said after the meeting. A 'memo' is a short note. A 'quorum' is the minimum number of members needed for a valid meeting.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the one word that can be substituted for the given group of words.
A speech delivered without any preparation

solution.concept: One-word substitution: speech terms
solution.explanation: An 'extempore' speech is delivered on the spot, without preparation.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Verbatim' means word for word. A 'soliloquy' is speaking one's thoughts aloud when alone, especially in a play. 'Rhetoric' is the art of persuasive speaking.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the one word that can be substituted for the given group of words.
The study of the origin and history of words

solution.concept: One-word substitution: fields of study
solution.explanation: 'Etymology' is the study of where words come from and how their forms and meanings have changed.
steps: Key words: origin and history of words
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Entomology' is the study of insects. 'Philology' is the broader study of language in historical texts. 'Lexicography' is the compiling of dictionaries.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The bank will open a new branch in our village next month.

options.text: A new branch would be opened in our village by the bank next month.
A new branch is opened in our village by the bank next month.
A new branch will be opened in our village by the bank next month.
A new branch will be open in our village by the bank next month.

solution.concept: Simple future active → will be + past participle
solution.explanation: 'Will open' becomes 'will be opened', the object 'a new branch' becomes the subject, and 'the bank' becomes the agent.
solution.why_others_wrong: A changes 'will' to 'would'. B changes the tense to present. D uses the adjective 'open' instead of the past participle 'opened'.
solution.final_answer: Option C: A new branch will be opened in our village by the bank next month.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
Do not touch the electric panel.

options.text: Let the electric panel not be touched.
The electric panel is not touched.
Let not the electric panel touched.
The electric panel should not touching.

solution.concept: Passive of a negative command: Let + object + not + be + past participle
solution.explanation: An imperative becomes passive with 'Let': 'Let the electric panel not be touched.'
solution.why_others_wrong: B turns the command into a statement of fact. C leaves out 'be'. D is ungrammatical ('should not touching').
solution.final_answer: Option A: Let the electric panel not be touched.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in indirect (reported) speech.
The customer said, "I want to close my account."

options.text: The customer said that he wants to close his account.
The customer said that I wanted to close my account.
The customer told that he wanted to close his account.
The customer said that he wanted to close his account.

solution.concept: Statement in reported speech: past reporting verb → backshift; first person → third person
solution.explanation: After 'said', the present 'want' moves back to 'wanted', and 'I/my' become 'he/his': 'The customer said that he wanted to close his account.'
solution.why_others_wrong: A keeps the present 'wants'. B keeps the first person 'I' and 'my'. C uses 'told' without an object ('told someone').
solution.final_answer: Option D: The customer said that he wanted to close his account.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in indirect (reported) speech.
The clerk asked me, "Have you brought your passbook?"

options.text: The clerk asked me had I brought my passbook.
The clerk asked me whether I had brought my passbook.
The clerk asked me whether I have brought my passbook.
The clerk asked me that whether I had brought my passbook.

solution.concept: Yes/no question in reported speech: 'whether/if' + statement order + backshift
solution.explanation: A yes/no question is reported with 'whether' (or 'if'), in statement order, with the present perfect moved back to the past perfect: 'whether I had brought my passbook'.
solution.why_others_wrong: A keeps question order. C does not backshift the tense. D adds 'that' before 'whether'.
solution.final_answer: Option B: The clerk asked me whether I had brought my passbook.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the verb form that correctly fills the blank.
The quality of the new currency notes ______ much better than that of the old ones.

solution.concept: The verb agrees with the head noun, not with a noun in the 'of' phrase
solution.explanation: The subject is 'quality' (singular); 'of the new currency notes' only describes it. So the verb is 'is'.
steps: 'of the new currency notes' is a modifier
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Are', 'have been' and 'were' are plural and wrongly agree with 'notes'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the verb form that correctly fills the blank.
Bread and butter ______ his usual breakfast before he leaves for the branch.

solution.concept: Two nouns joined by 'and' that form a single idea take a singular verb
solution.explanation: 'Bread and butter' here is one dish, a single idea, so it takes a singular verb: 'Bread and butter is his usual breakfast.' The singular complement 'his usual breakfast' confirms this.
steps: Do the two nouns name one item or two? One dish
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Are', 'have been' and 'were' are plural, which would treat bread and butter as two separate items, against the singular 'his usual breakfast'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the verb form that correctly fills the blank.
Not only the manager but also the clerks ______ responsible for the shortfall in the cash.

solution.concept: 'Not only ... but also': the verb agrees with the nearer subject
solution.explanation: With 'not only X but also Y', the verb agrees with Y, the subject nearer to it. Y is 'the clerks' (plural), so the verb is 'are'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Is', 'was' and 'has been' are singular and wrongly agree with 'the manager'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
The manager ______ just ______ the meeting, so you can see him now.

solution.concept: Present perfect with 'just' for a recently completed action that matters now
solution.explanation: The meeting ended a moment ago and the result is relevant now ('you can see him now'), so the present perfect is used: 'has just finished'.
steps: Clue: 'just' + present result 'you can see him now'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Had finished' is past perfect and needs a past reference point. 'Is just finishing' means it is not yet over, so he could not be seen now. 'Was just finished' is a passive form and does not fit.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
Our teacher told us that the earth ______ round the sun once a year.

solution.concept: Sequence of tenses: a universal truth stays in the present even after a past reporting verb
solution.explanation: Normally a past reporting verb ('told') moves the verb back. A universal or scientific truth is an exception and keeps the present tense: 'the earth goes round the sun'.
steps: But the reported fact is a permanent truth
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Went', 'had gone' and 'would go' backshift a permanent truth, which makes it sound as if it were true only in the past or in the future.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
He ______ for the bank for ten years when he was promoted to branch manager.

solution.concept: Past perfect continuous: an action continuing up to a point in the past
solution.explanation: The ten years of work continued up to a past event (his promotion). An action lasting until a past point takes the past perfect continuous: 'had been working for ten years when he was promoted'.
steps: Past reference point: 'when he was promoted'
Duration up to that point: 'for ten years'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Has been working' and 'is working' are present forms that clash with 'was promoted'. 'Was working' does not express a duration up to a past point with 'for ten years'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
______ sun rises in the east and sets in the west.

solution.concept: 'The' with things that are unique (the sun, the moon, the earth)
solution.explanation: There is only one sun, so it takes the definite article: 'The sun rises in the east.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'A' and 'An' suggest one of many suns. A singular countable noun like 'sun' cannot stand without an article here.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
______ rich are not always happier than ______ poor.

solution.concept: 'The' + adjective to refer to a whole class of people (the rich, the poor)
solution.explanation: 'The rich' and 'the poor' mean rich people and poor people as a class. This pattern needs 'the' + adjective, and the plural verb 'are' confirms it.
steps: Adjectives used as plural nouns for a class of people
solution.why_others_wrong: 'A rich' or 'a poor' cannot stand alone as nouns. Without an article, 'rich' and 'poor' cannot act as subjects or objects here. C mixes the forms.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
______ Ganga is ______ holy river for millions of people.

solution.concept: 'The' before names of rivers; 'a' for one member of a class
solution.explanation: Names of rivers take 'the' ('the Ganga'). The second blank describes the river as one of the class of holy rivers, so it takes 'a': 'a holy river'.
steps: Rivers take the definite article: 'The Ganga'
solution.why_others_wrong: A puts 'a' before a river's name. B ('the holy river') would mean the only holy river, which is not intended. C omits 'the' before the river's name.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.
Ever since she was a child, she has been fond ______ reading.

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: 'fond of'
solution.explanation: The adjective 'fond' takes 'of': 'fond of reading'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Fond with', 'fond for' and 'fond about' are not standard English.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.
The bank plans to ______ its old core-banking software over the next two years and move to a new system.

solution.concept: Phrasal verb 'phase out' = stop using something gradually
solution.explanation: The bank is moving to a new system, so the old software will be gradually withdrawn: 'phase out'.
steps: Context: replacing old software with a new system over two years
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Phase in' means introduce gradually, which suits the new system, not the old one. 'Bring up' (raise a topic) and 'set off' (start a journey, trigger) do not fit.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
______ the new queue-management software was installed, complaints about waiting time have fallen sharply.

solution.concept: Time connector 'ever since' + present perfect in the main clause
solution.explanation: The fall in complaints has continued from the time the software was installed. 'Ever since' marks the starting point, and the present perfect 'have fallen' confirms a period running up to now.
steps: Relation: the second event follows from and continues after the first
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Even though' sets up a contrast, but better software reducing complaints is expected, not surprising. 'Unless' (condition) and 'So that' (purpose) do not fit the relationship.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
The bank's profits fell this year because of higher provisions. ______, its asset quality improved, with bad loans at their lowest level in a decade.

solution.concept: Concession connector: a positive point despite a negative one
solution.explanation: Sentence 1 is negative (profits fell); sentence 2 is positive (asset quality improved). 'Nonetheless' introduces a point that holds in spite of the earlier one.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Consequently' and 'Hence' would make better asset quality a result of falling profits, which is not the logic. 'Similarly' signals a point of the same kind, but the second point is the opposite in tone.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Combine the two sentences into one, starting with 'Provided that'.
The borrower repays this loan on time. He will get a lower interest rate on his next loan.

options.text: Provided that the borrower will repay this loan on time, he gets a lower interest rate on his next loan.
Provided that the borrower repays this loan on time, but he will get a lower interest rate on his next loan.
Provided that repaying this loan on time, the borrower will get a lower interest rate on his next loan.
Provided that the borrower repays this loan on time, he will get a lower interest rate on his next loan.

solution.concept: 'Provided that' introduces a condition: present simple in the condition, 'will' in the result
solution.explanation: 'Provided that' works like 'if': the condition uses the present simple ('repays') and the result uses 'will' ('he will get').
steps: Result clause: 'will get', with no extra connector
solution.why_others_wrong: A uses 'will' in the condition clause and the present in the result. B adds 'but', which wrongly joins a condition to its result. C puts a participle after 'Provided that', which needs a full clause.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Provided that the borrower repays this loan on time, he will get a lower interest rate on his next loan.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
The scheme was meant to help small farmers; ______, most of its benefits went to large landowners.

solution.concept: Contrast between intention and outcome: 'in practice'
solution.explanation: The first clause states the intention; the second states what actually happened, which was different. 'In practice' introduces the real outcome as against the plan.
steps: Clause 1: what the scheme was meant to do
Connector of reality vs intention: 'in practice'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Accordingly' would make the outcome follow from the intention. 'Likewise' signals similarity. 'For instance' introduces an example, but clause 2 is not an example of clause 1.
